title: Given K sorted linked lists, merge them into one sorted linked list and return its head.
shortTitle: Merge K Sorted Lists — min-heap of K heads

s1_definition.profdef: Merge K Sorted Lists uses a min-heap holding the current head node of each list. Repeatedly extract the smallest head, append it to the output, and push that node's successor. Because the heap always surfaces the global minimum among the fronts, the output is produced in sorted order in n log K time, where n is the total node count.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine K sorted queues of pending settlements, each already ordered by time. To merge them into one master-ordered stream, you look only at the front of each queue, pick the earliest, move it to the master list, and advance that queue by one. A small priority board of K fronts tells you instantly which queue currently has the earliest item.
s1_definition.oneliner: Put the K list heads in a min-heap; repeatedly pop the smallest, append it, and push its next, giving a sorted merge in O(n log K).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Merge K Sorted Lists uses a min-heap holding the current head node of each list. Repeatedly extract the smallest head, append it to the output, and push that node's successor. Because the heap always surfaces the global minimum among the fronts, the output is produced in sorted order in n log K time, where n is the total node count.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine K sorted queues of pending settlements, each already ordered by time. To merge them into one master-ordered stream, you look only at the front of each queue, pick the earliest, move it to the master list, and advance that queue by one. A small priority board of K fronts tells you instantly which queue currently has the earliest item.

**One line to remember:** Put the K list heads in a min-heap; repeatedly pop the smallest, append it, and push its next, giving a sorted merge in O(n log K).

sections.s2_technical:
Seed a min-heap with the head of every non-empty list, ordered by node value. For example: `for (ListNode l : lists) if (l != null) heap.offer(l);`. The heap size never exceeds K.

Repeatedly poll the smallest node, append it to the tail of the result list, and if that node has a successor, push the successor into the heap. For example: `ListNode n = heap.poll(); tail.next = n; tail = n; if (n.next != null) heap.offer(n.next);`.

Continue until the heap is empty, at which point every node has been appended exactly once in nondecreasing order. A dummy head node simplifies appending by avoiding a special case for the first element. The total work is one heap push and pop per node, each costing log K, so the overall time is n log K and the extra space is K for the heap.

A senior nuance is that this beats the alternative of concatenating all lists and sorting, which is n log n, because the merge exploits the fact that each list is already sorted and only ever compares K fronts. An equally good alternative is pairwise divide-and-conquer merging, also n log K, which avoids a heap but uses recursion; the heap version is often clearer and naturally streaming.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, settlement events arrive from K regional systems, each stream already sorted by timestamp. The clearing engine must merge them into one globally time-ordered stream. This is exactly how Merge K Sorted Lists works — it merges pre-sorted streams by always taking the earliest front.

Problem 2 — The streams are long and must be merged without first sorting everything together. This is exactly why the min-heap of K heads is used, keeping only K fronts in memory at a time.

The mini-project builds a `SettlementMerger` with a `ListNode` and the heap merge, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo over three sorted streams.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three sorted streams: A with 100, 400, 700; B with 200, 500, 800; C with 150, 300, 900.

Step 1: The heap is seeded with the three heads 100, 200, 150. The smallest is 100 from A, which is appended and A advances to 400, pushed into the heap.

Step 2: The heap now holds 400, 200, 150. The smallest is 150 from C, appended, and C advances to 300, pushed.

Step 3: The heap holds 400, 200, 300. The smallest is 200 from B, appended, B advances to 500.

Step 4: The heap holds 400, 500, 300. The smallest is 300 from C, appended, C advances to 900.

Step 5: Continuing, the merge emits 400 from A, then 500 from B, then 700 from A, then 800 from B, then 900 from C, each time taking the earliest front and advancing that stream.

Step 6: When all streams are exhausted and the heap empties, the merged order is 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, 500, 700, 800, 900, globally sorted.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Merge K Sorted Lists asks me to combine K already-sorted lists into one sorted list. The naive idea of concatenating everything and sorting ignores that each list is already ordered and costs n log n. My efficient solution uses a min-heap holding the current head of each list, which lets me always find the global minimum among just the K fronts.

I seed the heap with every non-empty list head, then repeatedly poll the smallest node, append it to the output tail, and push that node's successor if it exists. Because the heap always surfaces the earliest front across all lists, the output comes out in sorted order. Each node is pushed and popped exactly once, each operation costing log K, so the total is n log K time with K extra space, and a dummy head node removes the special case for appending the first element.

The reason this beats sort-everything is that it compares only K fronts at a time rather than reordering all n elements, exploiting the per-list sorted property. I mention the equally efficient pairwise divide-and-conquer merge as an alternative with the same n log K bound, choosing the heap version because it is clear and naturally streaming.

In my project at National Bank of India, settlement events arrived from several regional systems, each stream already sorted by timestamp, and the clearing engine had to merge them into one globally time-ordered stream. The min-heap of K heads merged the long streams while holding only K fronts in memory, producing the master order in a single pass without ever sorting the combined volume from scratch.
